chief_complaint: trouble swallowing and feeling like food gets stuck in my chest
hpi_details: 28M with a history of allergic rhinitis and childhood asthma presents with progressive solid-food dysphagia over the last 2 years. He reports three episodes of food impaction requiring him to regurgitate. He denies weight loss, vomiting blood, or heartburn. He has noticed that eating slower and drinking lots of water helps him swallow.
ideas: thinks his throat is narrowing from some kind of scar tissue
concerns: terrified of choking to death while eating
expectations: hopes for an imaging test to see what's blocking his throat
social_hx: Software engineer, social drinker, no tobacco use

core_concepts: Eosinophilic esophagitis is a chronic, immune-mediated disease characterized clinically by esophageal dysfunction and histologically by eosinophil-predominant inflammation.
Most commonly seen in young males with a personal or family history of atopy.
The classic presentation is solid-food dysphagia and episodes of food impaction.
Diagnosis requires endoscopy showing typical features (rings, furrows, exudates) and biopsies with >=15 eosinophils/hpf.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: trouble swallowing and feeling like food gets stuck in my chest
Key HPI features: 28M with atopic history experiencing progressive solid-food dysphagia and food impaction without typical GERD symptoms.
Objective/Exam findings: Vitals normal. Physical exam is generally unremarkable. The key to diagnosis is history and subsequent endoscopy.
Relevant background/PMH: Allergic rhinitis, asthma (Atopic triad)
common_misconceptions: Assuming all dysphagia in young people is strictly due to GERD or anxiety.
Delaying endoscopy and trying prolonged blind PPI therapy without investigating for EoE in highly suspicious cases.
Ignoring the patient's atopic history which is a major risk factor.
dangerous_errors: Attempting blind esophageal dilation before confirming the diagnosis, which can lead to high risk of esophageal perforation in EoE.
Failing to refer to gastroenterology for urgent endoscopy in the setting of acute food impaction.
management_principles: Refer to Gastroenterology for upper endoscopy with esophageal biopsies.
Initial treatment options include Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs), swallowed topical corticosteroids (e.g., fluticasone or budesonide), and dietary elimination therapies.
Allergist consultation for potential food allergy testing, though empiric elimination diets are often preferred.
boundaries_and_exceptions: PPI therapy can be effective in EoE and is no longer just used to rule out GERD.
Patients with acute food impaction require emergent endoscopy.

reference_soap.subjective: 28M with a history of atopy presents with a 2-year history of solid-food dysphagia and recurrent food impactions. No red flag symptoms like weight loss or hematemesis.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals stable. General appearance is healthy. Oropharynx clear. Abdomen soft, non-tender.
reference_soap.assessment: Solid-food dysphagia highly suspicious for Eosinophilic Esophagitis (EoE), given the patient's atopic history.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Refer to Gastroenterology for upper endoscopy and esophageal biopsies (requesting multi-level biopsies to check for eosinophils). 2. Start a trial of oral PPI (Omeprazole 20mg twice daily). 3. Advise the patient to chew food thoroughly, eat slowly, and seek emergency care immediately if food becomes completely impacted and cannot be cleared. 4. Outpatient Allergy/Immunology follow-up for potential dietary elimination guidance.

learning_objectives: Recognize the clinical presentation of EoE in young, atopic adults
Identify solid-food dysphagia and food impaction as key symptoms
Formulate an appropriate referral plan for endoscopy and biopsy

teaching.one_liner: An allergic inflammation of the esophagus causing swallowing difficulties and food impaction, typically in young men with asthma or allergies.
differentials: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) with peptic stricture
red_flags: Inability to swallow liquids or saliva (indicates complete acute obstruction needing emergent endoscopy)
Significant weight loss or hematemesis (suggests malignancy or severe ulceration)

must_ask.say: Do you have trouble swallowing solids, liquids, or both?
Can you swallow your own saliva right now?
Do you have any history of asthma, eczema, or environmental allergies?

history.answer: I've been having trouble swallowing, and it feels like food keeps getting stuck in my chest.
It started about two years ago, and it has been gradually happening more often over time.
I can initiate the swallow fine in my mouth, but a few seconds later food feels stuck right behind my breastbone.
It's only with solid foods like meat and dense bread; liquids like water go down with no problem.
Yes, I've had three episodes where food got completely stuck and wouldn't budge, so I had to make myself throw it up.
I've learned to eat much slower and drink lots of water between bites, which helps wash the food down.
Right now I can swallow my saliva and water just fine, so my throat isn't completely blocked today.
No, I don't cough or choke when I swallow, food never comes out my nose, and I haven't had pneumonia.
I don't bring up undigested food between meals, I have no bad breath, and there are no gurgling noises in my neck.
No sharp pain when I swallow, just a tight, uncomfortable pressure when food gets stuck.
No, I don't suffer from chronic heartburn or sour acid rising into my throat.
No, I haven't had any squeezing or crushing chest pains.
My appetite has been fine and I haven't lost any weight over these two years.
No, I haven't vomited blood, and my bowel movements are normal brown with no black stools.
No, my voice hasn't become hoarse or changed at all.
No slurred speech, facial weakness, drooping eyelids, double vision, arm or leg weakness, or tremors.
I have had allergic rhinitis for years and had asthma as a child, but no known food allergies.
No, I don't take pills without water or right before lying down in bed, and my immune system is healthy.
No, my fingers don't change color in the cold, and my skin doesn't feel tight or stiff.
No, I haven't felt any lumps, bumps, or swelling anywhere in my neck.
I honestly think my food pipe is narrowing down from some kind of scar tissue.
I'm terrified that one day I might choke to death while eating.
I'm hoping to get an imaging test or a camera look down my throat to see what's blocking it.
Other than allergic rhinitis and childhood asthma, I've had no other chronic illnesses.
I've never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I only use fluticasone nasal spray as needed for my allergies, and no other medications.
No, I have no known drug allergies.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco.
I drink socially, maybe a beer or two occasionally with friends.
I work as a software engineer and live alone in an apartment.
My mother has asthma and eczema, but there's no family history of throat or stomach cancers.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 120/78 mmHg, heart rate is 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 14 breaths per minute, body temperature is 36.7°C, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air.
Well-nourished, comfortable young male in no acute distress with normal hydration status.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor, and sclerae are anicteric.
Oropharynx is clear without mucosal lesions, candidal plaques, or tonsillar exudates, and dentition is intact.
No cervical, supraclavicular, or submandibular lymphadenopathy palpated.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, smooth, and non-tender without palpable nodules.
Palatal elevation is symmetric, gag reflex is intact, tongue moves normally, and patient swallows water cleanly without coughing.
Breath sounds are clear bilaterally with no wheezes, rhonchi, or crackles.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender throughout with no palpable epigastric mass or hepatosplenomegaly.
Skin is warm and dry without rash, eczema, or sclerodactyly.
